title: What authentication is
idea: Authentication is a login system: the user proves a secret once, and the server hands back proof that works for later requests.
points: HTTP forgets you between requests, so the server must recognize you again.
A hash is a one-way scramble of the password; sign-up stores only that.
bcrypt mixes in a random salt, so one password gives different hashes.
The proof, a cookie or token, replaces the password on later requests.

hero.title: A login story: Ada and the Book Store

items.label: Sign up
items.text: Ada picks a password. The server stores only its hash.

items.label: Log in
items.text: Ada sends email and password. The server hashes the attempt and compares.

items.label: Receive proof
items.text: On a match the server answers with proof, such as a cookie.

items.label: Show proof
items.text: Every later request carries the proof. The password is never sent again.

items.label: Log out
items.text: The proof is discarded or revoked, so the next request is a stranger's.

code.title: Sign up and log in
code.caption: `bcryptjs` is pure JavaScript with the same API as the native `bcrypt` package. Step through, then press Run.

walk.text: A `Map` stands in for the users table: email to stored hash.
Sign-up stores only the hash. The `10` is the cost: higher is slower, for attackers too.
An unknown email has no hash and fails. Otherwise `compare` hashes the attempt with the stored salt.
Two users sign up with the same password.
Three attempts: right password, wrong password, unknown email.
Compare the two stored hashes. Each has its own random salt, so predict the result.

pitfalls: Never store or log a plain password. Keep only the bcrypt hash.
Do not hash passwords with SHA-256 or MD5; fast hashes make guessing cheap.
Hashing the attempt again and using `===` never matches. Call `bcrypt.compare`.

quiz.why: `compare` re-hashes the attempt with the salt inside the stored hash. Case matters, and the stored value is a hash, not the password.

takeaway: Verify the secret once, then recognize the user by proof, not the password.
